title: Who Needs What: Recreational TRUST vs Part 107 Certification
html:
Two legal lanes, one airspace

Every drone flight in US national airspace falls into one of two regulatory lanes, and choosing the wrong one is the most common rookie mistake. The lane is decided not by your aircraft but by your intent and the nature of the operation. Get this wrong and an otherwise perfect flight is illegal.

Lane one is recreational flying under the statutory exception for limited recreational operations (often called 49 U.S.C. 44809). This covers flying strictly for personal enjoyment with no business purpose. Lane two is Part 107, the FAA rule for any non-recreational drone operation, which the FAA calls a commercial or civil operation.

Law.
Rules change. This lesson teaches the framework; before you fly, confirm the current text of 14 CFR Part 107 and the recreational exception on faa.gov and read the latest Advisory Circulars. Do not rely on any course as legal authority.

The recreational lane and TRUST

If you fly purely for fun, you must pass TRUST (The Recreational UAS Safety Test). TRUST is free, online, has no expiration, and you cannot fail it permanently because it teaches as it tests. You keep the completion certificate and present it on request. Recreational flyers must also follow the safety guidelines of an FAA-recognized Community Based Organization (CBO), fly within visual line of sight, and register the drone if it is over 0.55 lb (250 g).

What counts as recreational is narrow. The classic FAA example: photographing your own backyard for fun is recreational; the moment you post that footage to monetize a channel, sell the image, or shoot it for a client, you have crossed into Part 107 territory. Compensation is not required to make a flight non-recreational. If the flight furthers a business in any way, it is a Part 107 operation.

The Part 107 lane

Part 107 requires a Remote Pilot Certificate. You earn it by passing the Unmanned Aircraft General (UAG) knowledge test at an FAA-approved testing center, then completing FAA Form 8710-13 through IACRA. You must be at least 16, able to read/speak/write/understand English, and in a physical and mental condition to fly safely. The certificate unlocks operations the recreational lane forbids and prohibits or restricts: flying for any business purpose, applying for waivers, and operating under documented authorizations.

Which lane? decision checklist
Ask in order: 1. Is the flight strictly for personal fun, no business tie? -> Recreational (TRUST). 2. Any commercial, business, or compensated purpose? -> Part 107. 3. Unsure or mixed purpose? -> Fly under Part 107; it is the stricter, safer default. Either lane: register drones over 250 g, maintain VLOS, check airspace.

Registration and Remote ID

Both lanes intersect with two more requirements. Registration via FAA DroneZone is required for any drone over 250 g (recreational registration covers all your drones under one number; Part 107 requires per-aircraft registration). Remote ID broadcast is now required for most drones that must be registered, via a standard built-in module or an add-on broadcast module, with limited exceptions like flying inside an FAA-Recognized Identification Area.

Tip.
When in doubt, get your Part 107 certificate. It is the superset: a Part 107 pilot can legally do everything a recreational flyer can, plus operate commercially. Many serious hobbyists certify just to remove ambiguity.
▸Exercise

Classify five scenarios into the correct lane and justify each.

  1. You fly your 249 g drone to film a sunset for your personal photo album.
  2. A neighbor offers you $50 to photograph their roof; you accept.
  3. You film a wedding for free as a favor to a friend who is a professional planner using it in her portfolio.
  4. A 900 g drone flown only at a club field for fun.
  5. You post hobby footage to a monetized YouTube channel.

For each, state the lane, the certificate needed, and whether registration applies.

Quiz

Knowledge check
Q1. A real-estate agent asks you to photograph a house. You do it unpaid as a favor. Which lane? A: Part 107. The flight furthers a business; compensation is irrelevant. Recreational requires a purely personal purpose. Q2. What test does a purely-for-fun flyer of a 500 g drone need? A: TRUST, plus FAA registration because the drone exceeds 250 g. Q3. Minimum age for a Remote Pilot Certificate? A: 16 years old.

title: The Airspace System: Classes B, C, D, E, and G for Drones
html:
Why the alphabet matters

US airspace is divided into classes that describe how tightly air traffic is controlled. For a drone pilot the practical question is simple: do I need authorization to fly here, and up to what altitude? Part 107 caps you at 400 feet AGL anyway (with the structure exception), but the controlled-vs-uncontrolled distinction decides whether you may launch at all without a green light.

The big mental model: controlled airspace (B, C, D, and surface-area E) requires ATC authorization before a Part 107 drone flight. Uncontrolled airspace (Class G) does not require authorization, though all the other rules still apply.

Law.
Authorization requirements and airspace boundaries change. Always verify against current FAA charts, NOTAMs, and the latest Part 107 text before flight. This is study material, not clearance.

Class by class

Airspace cheat sheet (drone view)
Class B - Busy major airports (upside-down wedding cake) Authorization REQUIRED. Densest traffic. LAANC often available; some areas need manual request. Class C - Medium airports with radar approach Authorization REQUIRED. Typically 5 NM core, shelf to 10 NM. Class D - Towered airports, smaller Authorization REQUIRED. Roughly 4 NM radius surface to ~2,500 ft. Class E - Controlled, often starts at 700 or 1,200 ft AGL Authorization REQUIRED only where Class E touches the SURFACE (E2/surface area). Elsewhere E above you is usually fine for a 400 ft drone. Class G - Uncontrolled No authorization needed. Most rural flying. Still obey all other rules.

Class B: the upside-down wedding cake

Class B surrounds the busiest airports (think major international hubs). On a sectional it is drawn with solid blue lines forming a tiered, inverted-wedding-cake shape: a small surface circle, then wider rings at higher floors. A drone under any tier still needs authorization for that area. The numbers in each ring (like 100/SFC) read ceiling-over-floor in hundreds of feet MSL; SFC means surface.

Class C and D

Class C uses solid magenta lines and surrounds airports with radar service. Class D uses dashed blue lines and surrounds smaller towered airports; a segmented number box gives its ceiling in hundreds of feet MSL (e.g., [25] = 2,500 ft MSL). Both require authorization for drones.

Class E and G: the subtle ones

Class E is controlled airspace that usually does not touch the ground. The dashed magenta line marks Class E that extends to the surface (a surface area, sometimes around a non-towered airport with instrument approaches) and DOES require authorization. The faded magenta gradient (the soft shading) marks Class E starting at 700 ft AGL; the faded blue gradient marks 1,200 ft AGL. Because you fly at or below 400 ft, that overlying E rarely affects you. Class G is everything left over near the surface in less-busy areas, requiring no authorization.

Tip.
Confused by colors? Memorize: solid blue = B, solid magenta = C, dashed blue = D, dashed magenta = E to surface (authorization!), faded magenta = E at 700 AGL, no marking near surface = G.
▸Exercise

Pick your home location in the B4UFLY or Aloft app. Identify the airspace class at the surface where you live, whether authorization is required, and the nearest controlled airspace boundary. Write a one-line pre-flight authorization decision.

  1. Open the app and drop a pin on your usual launch site.
  2. Note the class and any altitude grid value (the LAANC ceiling, like 0, 100, 200, 400 ft).
  3. State whether you can self-authorize via LAANC or must request manually.

Quiz

Knowledge check
Q1. You see a dashed magenta circle around a small airport on the sectional. Authorization needed? A: Yes. Dashed magenta = Class E to the surface, which is controlled airspace requiring authorization. Q2. The faded magenta shading over a rural field means Class E begins at what altitude? A: 700 ft AGL. Since you fly at/below 400 ft, it does not require authorization. Q3. Which class generally needs NO authorization for a Part 107 drone? A: Class G (uncontrolled).

title: Reading VFR Sectional Charts: Symbols, Floors, and Frequencies
html:
The chart is the test

A large share of the Part 107 knowledge test is chart reading. The FAA hands you a VFR sectional chart legend in the supplement booklet, so you do not memorize every symbol, but you must read fluently and fast. A sectional packs airspace, terrain, obstacles, airports, and radio frequencies into a dense color-coded picture.

Law.
Chart symbology is periodically revised. Practice on current FAA sectionals and the current Chart Supplement. Always cross-check with NOTAMs for temporary changes.

Airspace lines and floors/ceilings

Revisit the line colors from the last lesson, then add the number conventions. A ceiling/floor stack like 55/12 means top at 5,500 ft MSL, bottom at 1,200 ft MSL. SFC means the floor is the surface. A Class D ceiling appears as a dashed-box number such as [27] = 2,700 ft MSL. Class C shelves list both numbers, e.g., 41/18.

Airport symbols

Airports in blue have a control tower; airports in magenta do not. Small tick marks around the airport circle indicate fuel availability; an enclosed box with a small R or runway depiction conveys runway layout. A star above the airport symbol indicates a rotating beacon. The airport data block lists the name, elevation, and the longest runway length.

Decoding a sample data block
RIVERTON (RIV) CT - 119.4 *L 82 35 122.95 RIVERTON (RIV): airport name and identifier. CT - 119.4: Control Tower frequency 119.4 (blue = towered). *L: lighting available, * = part-time/see remarks. 82: field elevation 82 ft MSL. 35: longest runway 3,500 ft (hundreds of feet). 122.95: a UNICOM/CTAF advisory frequency.

Frequencies that matter

For a drone pilot the key frequency is the CTAF (Common Traffic Advisory Frequency), often marked with a magenta C in a circle. While you do not transmit, knowing where crewed traffic announces helps situational awareness and answers test questions. Tower (CT), ground, ATIS, and AWOS/ASOS weather frequencies also appear in the chart and Chart Supplement.

Obstacles, terrain, and special-use airspace

Obstacles are little tower icons; tall ones (1,000 ft AGL or more) get a thicker symbol, and the numbers give height in MSL (bold) and AGL (parentheses) - for example 1149 (453) means the top is 1,149 ft MSL, 453 ft above ground. A small flag near groups of obstacles warns of a wind farm or congested obstruction field. Terrain elevation is shown with color tints and a maximum-elevation figure (MEF) in each quadrangle.

Special-use airspace (SUA) appears in distinctive hatched borders: blue hatching for Prohibited (P), Restricted (R), and Warning areas; blue or magenta for MOAs (Military Operations Areas), and dashed blue for Alert/National Security Areas. A boundary box on the chart edge lists each SUA's altitudes, times of use, and the controlling agency. Prohibited and Restricted areas can be off-limits; even MOAs warrant caution.

Tip.
On the test, work backwards: read the question first, then scan only the chart region it asks about. Most chart questions hinge on one symbol or one number - find it and ignore the rest.
▸Exercise

Print or open any FAA VFR sectional excerpt and a legend, then answer for one airport:

  1. Is it towered or non-towered, and how do you know?
  2. What is the field elevation and longest runway length?
  3. What is the CTAF, and what airspace class touches the surface there?
  4. Identify one obstacle within 5 NM and state its MSL and AGL heights.

Quiz

Knowledge check
Q1. An airport symbol is magenta. What does color tell you? A: Magenta = non-towered airport. Blue = towered. Q2. An obstacle reads 2210 (1209). What is its height above ground? A: 1,209 ft AGL. The bold number (2,210) is MSL; the parenthetical is AGL. Q3. A blue-hatched area labeled R-2304 with a boundary box. What is it? A: A Restricted Area; check the boundary box for altitudes, hours, and controlling agency before going near it.

title: Airspace Authorizations, LAANC, and Waivers
html:
From red zone to cleared

When you need to fly in controlled airspace, you need authorization. The FAA built LAANC (Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability) to make routine approvals nearly instant, and reserved a slower DroneZone manual process and the formal waiver process for everything else.

Law.
LAANC providers, grid altitudes, and waiver categories evolve. Verify current LAANC coverage and the FAA DroneZone process before relying on this lesson operationally.

LAANC: the fast lane

LAANC is a partnership between the FAA and approved app providers (such as Aloft, Avision, and others). It works against UAS Facility Maps (UASFMs) - grids over controlled airspace where each cell shows a pre-approved maximum altitude (0, 100, 200, 300, or 400 ft). If your request is at or below the grid ceiling, LAANC can grant authorization in near real time.

LAANC vs manual authorization
Request at/below grid ceiling, standard hours: LAANC auto-approval, often seconds. Best for routine jobs. Request ABOVE the grid ceiling, or in a zero-grid cell: Cannot self-authorize. Submit a Further Coordination / manual request via DroneZone; can take weeks. Recurring need in same spot: Consider a long-term LAANC authorization or a waiver.

A grid value of zero

A grid cell of 0 does not mean you can never fly - it means LAANC will not auto-approve there (usually right next to a runway). You must request manually through DroneZone and wait for FAA review. Treat any zero-grid as a stop sign for same-day work.

Waivers: breaking a rule, safely

A waiver is FAA permission to deviate from specific Part 107 operating rules when you prove you can still operate safely. You apply through DroneZone with a detailed safety case and concept of operations. Common waivable rules include:

  • Operating beyond visual line of sight (BVLOS) - the hardest to obtain.
  • Operating over people beyond what the operations-over-people rule permits.
  • Operating at night (note: night ops are now allowed under the rule with training and lighting, so a waiver is needed only for parts the rule does not cover).
  • Operation of multiple aircraft by one pilot.
  • Operating from a moving vehicle beyond allowed conditions, or above 400 ft, or exceeding speed limits.

Note that some operating limitations - like the requirement to maintain VLOS or the daylight rule - can be waived, but the airspace authorization requirement itself is satisfied through LAANC/DroneZone authorization, not a waiver. Know the difference: authorization gives you access to controlled airspace; a waiver lifts an operating restriction.

Tip.
Build your waiver request like a safety engineer: identify the hazard each rule mitigates, then describe specifically how your procedures, equipment, and crew restore that safety margin. Vague applications get denied.
▸Exercise

Plan an authorization for a hypothetical rooftop inspection in Class D airspace, 250 ft AGL, where the UASFM grid shows 200 ft at your cell.

  1. Decide: can you use LAANC, or must you go manual? Why?
  2. List exactly what data the request needs (location, altitude, time window, duration).
  3. Write the one rule you would have to request manually around, and the safety mitigation you would cite.

Quiz

Knowledge check
Q1. The UASFM grid at your site reads 0 ft. What does that mean for same-day flight? A: No LAANC auto-approval. You must submit a manual request via DroneZone and wait for FAA review. Q2. You want to fly BVLOS commercially. Authorization or waiver? A: Waiver. BVLOS deviates from an operating rule, so it requires a Part 107 waiver with a safety case. Q3. What does a LAANC grid number represent? A: The pre-approved maximum AGL altitude for auto-authorization in that cell.

title: Aviation Weather: METAR, TAF, Density Altitude, and Micrometeorology
html:
Weather is a graded subject

The knowledge test treats weather seriously because weather causes accidents. You must read coded reports, understand how heat and humidity rob performance, and anticipate how terrain twists the wind near the ground where drones actually fly.

Law.
Always get a current weather briefing before flight. Coded formats and reporting standards can change; practice on live data from aviationweather.gov.

Reading a METAR

A METAR is an observation of current conditions; a TAF is a forecast for an airport's vicinity. Decode left to right.

METAR decode
KORD 121651Z 24015G25KT 6SM BKN030 OVC050 28/19 A2992 KORD: station (Chicago O'Hare). 121651Z: 12th day, 1651 ZULU (UTC) time. 24015G25KT: wind from 240 deg at 15 kt, gusting 25 kt. 6SM: visibility 6 statute miles. BKN030 OVC050: broken clouds 3,000 ft AGL, overcast 5,000 ft AGL. 28/19: temperature 28 C, dewpoint 19 C. A2992: altimeter 29.92 inHg. Cloud cover: SKC/CLR clear, FEW, SCT scattered, BKN broken, OVC overcast.

Why the temperature/dewpoint spread matters

The closer temperature and dewpoint are, the more saturated the air and the higher the chance of fog or low clouds. A small spread that is shrinking is a fog warning. Estimate cloud base roughly: spread in C divided by 2.5, times 1,000, gives feet AGL to the convective cloud base. A 28/19 spread (9 C) suggests bases far above the surface; a 18/17 spread screams imminent fog.

Density altitude: the silent performance thief

Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for non-standard temperature - effectively the altitude your aircraft feels like it is flying at. High, hot, and humid all raise density altitude. Thin air means less lift and less propeller bite, so your drone climbs slower, hovers harder, and drains battery faster. On a hot day at elevation, a drone that screams at sea level may struggle to maintain altitude. Plan shorter flights and lower payloads in those conditions.

Tip.
Remember the phrase 'high, hot, and humid hurts.' All three increase density altitude and degrade performance. If two of the three are present, build in extra battery and altitude margin.

Micrometeorology near terrain

Drones live in the boundary layer, where the ground rewrites the wind. Key effects: mechanical turbulence and rotors downwind of buildings, ridges, and tree lines; venturi acceleration as wind squeezes through gaps, canyons, and between buildings; thermals and convective lift over hot surfaces like parking lots; and katabatic/anabatic flow as air drains down or climbs slopes with the daily heating cycle. Expect the worst turbulence on the lee (downwind) side of obstacles and the strongest gusts in the squeeze points. Approaching a ridge from the lee side can put you in sinking, rotor-filled air.

Temperature inversions and stability

A surface inversion (warm air over cool) traps haze and smooth but sometimes surprising wind shear aloft. Stable air gives smooth flight but poor visibility; unstable air gives good visibility but bumps, gusts, and building cumulus. The test likes the association: stable = stratus, smooth, restricted visibility; unstable = cumulus, turbulence, showers, good visibility.

▸Exercise

Pull a live METAR for your nearest airport and analyze it for a drone flight.

  1. Decode wind, gust, visibility, ceiling, temp/dewpoint, altimeter.
  2. Compute the temp/dewpoint spread and judge fog risk.
  3. State whether the ceiling and visibility meet Part 107 weather minimums (3 SM visibility, 500 ft below / 2,000 ft horizontal from clouds).
  4. Identify one terrain or building feature near your site that would create turbulence today given the wind direction.

Quiz

Knowledge check
Q1. In 24015G25KT, what is the gust value? A: 25 knots (G25). Steady wind is 15 kt from 240 degrees. Q2. Which conditions raise density altitude and hurt performance? A: High elevation, high temperature, and high humidity - 'high, hot, and humid.' Q3. A METAR reads 17/16. What weather should you anticipate? A: A 1 C spread means near-saturation: expect fog or low stratus and reduced visibility.

title: Loading, Performance, and Crew Resource Management
html:
The aircraft you actually have today

Performance is not a spec sheet number; it is the spec sheet adjusted for today's weight, weather, and wear. Part 107 tests whether you understand how loading and conditions change what your aircraft can do, and how a crew works together to catch errors.

Law.
Follow the manufacturer's published limits and the current Part 107 rules. Treat this as the reasoning framework, not a substitute for your aircraft's manual.

Weight, balance, and center of gravity

Adding a payload (camera gimbal, sensor, delivery package) increases weight and shifts the center of gravity. Heavier means slower climb, longer braking distance, higher stall/translational speed for fixed-wing, shorter flight time, and a smaller margin against gusts. A CG too far from the design point makes the aircraft sluggish or twitchy and forces the flight controller to fight it, burning more current. Always mount payloads at the recommended balance point and stay under the maximum takeoff weight.

Load and performance effects
Add weight -> slower climb, shorter endurance, higher current draw, longer stopping distance. High density altitude (hot/high/humid) -> less lift and thrust; compounds a heavy load. Off-center CG -> poor handling, wasted battery fighting trim. Mitigation: lighten payload, balance correctly, fly cooler/lower, plan shorter legs.

Battery and the reserve mindset

Battery is your fuel, and like fuel it must include a reserve. Cold reduces usable capacity; high current draw from heavy loads or aggressive flight sags voltage early. Land with margin - never chase the last percent. Wind matters too: a downwind leg outbound can leave you fighting a headwind home with a depleted pack, the classic way to run out of energy short of the landing zone.

Crew Resource Management

CRM is the disciplined use of all available resources - people, equipment, information - to operate safely. Even a solo operator practices a version of it through checklists and self-discipline, but Part 107 explicitly allows a crew, and the test asks about roles.

  • Remote Pilot in Command (RPIC): legally responsible for the flight, final authority, must be able to take control instantly.
  • Person Manipulating the Controls: may fly under the RPIC's direct supervision if the RPIC can immediately take over.
  • Visual Observer (VO): helps maintain VLOS and scans for traffic and hazards, communicating continuously with the RPIC.

Good CRM means clear communication, defined roles, a sterile-cockpit attitude during critical phases, and a culture where any crew member can call 'knock it off' to abort. Aeronautical Decision Making (ADM) is the partner skill: a systematic approach to consistently choosing the safest course of action. The test highlights the five hazardous attitudes and their antidotes.

Five hazardous attitudes & antidotes
Anti-authority ('Don't tell me') -> Follow the rules; they are usually right. Impulsivity ('Do something quick') -> Not so fast; think first. Invulnerability ('It won't happen to me') -> It could happen to me. Macho ('I can do it') -> Taking chances is foolish. Resignation ('What's the use') -> I'm not helpless; I can make a difference.
Tip.
Use the IMSAFE personal checklist before flying: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion/Eating. A grounded pilot who feels off is practicing the best CRM of all.
▸Exercise

Build a two-person crew brief for a survey flight with an added 200 g sensor on a hot day.

  1. Assign RPIC and VO roles and the exact phrase to abort.
  2. List three performance effects of the added weight plus heat, and your mitigations.
  3. Set a battery landing threshold (percent or voltage) accounting for the headwind home.
  4. Run an IMSAFE self-check and note any item that would scrub the flight.

Quiz

Knowledge check
Q1. Adding payload near the maximum takeoff weight most directly causes what? A: Reduced climb performance and endurance, with higher current draw and longer stopping distance. Q2. The antidote to the 'macho' hazardous attitude is? A: 'Taking chances is foolish.' Q3. Who holds final authority and responsibility for the flight? A: The Remote Pilot in Command (RPIC).

title: The Operating Rules: VLOS, Night, Over People, and Special Ops
html:
The rules you fly by

Once certified, you operate inside a box of rules. The test probes the box edges relentlessly, because most violations come from misunderstanding a limit. Memorize the core operating limitations of Part 107 - and remember that several can be waived with FAA approval.

Law.
Operating rules, especially night, over-people, and Remote ID provisions, have changed in recent years and may change again. Confirm the current 14 CFR Part 107 text before operating.

Core limitations

Part 107 core operating limits
Max altitude: 400 ft AGL (or within 400 ft of a structure when inspecting it). Max groundspeed: 100 mph (87 knots). Min visibility: 3 statute miles from the control station. Cloud clearance: 500 ft below, 2,000 ft horizontal. VLOS: maintain visual line of sight with the unaided eye (corrective lenses ok). One aircraft per pilot unless waived. No careless/reckless operation; no carrying hazardous materials; no dropping objects that create a hazard.

VLOS in detail

Visual line of sight means you (or your VO) can see the aircraft with unaided vision well enough to know its location, orientation, altitude, and attitude, and to scan for traffic and hazards. Binoculars and FPV goggles do not satisfy VLOS - if you fly FPV, a VO must maintain unaided VLOS. Momentary glances at the controller or to scan for traffic are acceptable; sustained loss of sight is not.

Daylight and night

Operations are permitted during daylight and civil twilight, and at night provided the remote pilot has completed the updated training/knowledge requirement and the aircraft displays anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles with a flash rate sufficient to avoid a collision. Civil twilight operations also require that lighting. Know that the night allowance came with this lighting and training condition.

Operations over people and moving vehicles

The over-people rule sorts drones into categories based on injury potential:

  • Category 1: very light drones (under 0.55 lb / 250 g) with no exposed parts that could lacerate - may operate over people if other conditions are met.
  • Category 2: heavier drones that meet an injury threshold and have no lacerating parts, with a manufacturer declaration of compliance.
  • Category 3: higher injury threshold; restricted from sustained flight over open-air assemblies and limited to closed/restricted sites or transiting people briefly.
  • Category 4: drones with an airworthiness certificate operated per their approval.

Operations over moving vehicles are likewise restricted: you generally may not fly sustained over moving vehicles unless within a closed or restricted-access site, or the operation meets the relevant category and transit conditions. Remote ID broadcast is also required for most over-people operations.

Danger.
Never assume an operation over a crowd is legal because your drone is small. Open-air assemblies (concerts, sporting events) carry the strictest limits, and many also fall under Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs). Check NOTAMs every time.

Waivers and special operations

Several limits above can be lifted by an FAA waiver: BVLOS, multiple aircraft per pilot, over-people beyond category limits, from a moving vehicle beyond allowed conditions, and operations exceeding speed or altitude. The waiver demands a safety case. Treat any unwaived deviation as a violation regardless of how safe it felt.

▸Exercise

Audit a planned twilight rooftop shoot over a parking lot with occasional pedestrians.

  1. List every core limit that applies and your compliance status for each.
  2. Decide whether the over-people category permits transiting the pedestrians, or whether you must keep them clear.
  3. State the lighting requirement for the twilight portion.
  4. Identify which, if any, rule would need a waiver, and why.

Quiz

Knowledge check
Q1. May you satisfy VLOS using FPV goggles alone? A: No. FPV requires a visual observer maintaining unaided VLOS. Q2. What lighting is required to fly at night under Part 107? A: Anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles with an effective flash rate, plus completion of the night training. Q3. Maximum allowable groundspeed under Part 107? A: 100 mph (87 knots).

title: The Knowledge-Test Domains and a Concrete Study Plan
html:
Know the shape of the exam

The Part 107 Unmanned Aircraft General (UAG) knowledge test is a proctored, computer-based exam of 60 multiple-choice questions, each with three answer choices, and you need 70% to pass. You have a generous time window (around 2 hours) and a printed supplement booklet with charts and figures. Going in knowing the domains lets you study efficiently instead of cramming randomly.

Law.
Question count, weighting, and passing standards can be revised. Confirm current test specifications in the FAA's Airman Certification Standards for the UAG before you schedule.

The tested domains

Approximate domain weighting
Regulations (Part 107, operating rules, certification): largest share, ~15-25%. Airspace classification & operating requirements: ~15-25%. Weather sources & effects on performance: ~11-16%. Loading & performance: ~7-11%. Operations (CRM, ADM, physiology, radio, maintenance, night): ~35-45%. Exact percentages vary; the FAA ACS is authoritative.

The biggest point pools

Two areas reward study most: chart/airspace reading and regulations. Together they can approach half the exam, and they are the most learnable - they are rules and symbols, not judgment calls. Weather is the next-best return. Loading is small but easy points. The 'operations' bucket is broad: CRM, aeronautical decision making, the hazardous attitudes, aeromedical factors (dehydration, hypoxia at altitude, vision, drugs/alcohol), radio phraseology basics, and airport operations.

A four-week study plan

  1. Week 1 - Regulations and certification. Read Part 107 itself, the recreational exception, and the certification process. Make flashcards for every numeric limit.
  2. Week 2 - Airspace and charts. Drill sectional symbology daily. Do 20 chart questions a day with the legend until the colors and numbers are reflexive.
  3. Week 3 - Weather, loading, performance. Decode five METARs and a TAF daily. Master density altitude and the temp/dewpoint relationship.
  4. Week 4 - Operations and full mocks. Cover CRM, ADM, aeromedical, radio, night. Take full 60-question timed practice tests; review every miss until you know why the wrong answers are wrong.
Tip.
Track your practice-test scores. Schedule the real exam only after you consistently score 85%+ on fresh mock tests - that cushion absorbs test-day nerves and the inevitable trick question.

Sample questions in the FAA style

FAA-style sample items
Q. (Refer to a sectional) The floor of Class E shown by faded magenta shading is: A) the surface B) 700 ft AGL C) 1,200 ft AGL Answer B. Faded magenta = Class E starting at 700 ft AGL. Q. Maximum altitude under Part 107 over open terrain is: A) 400 ft AGL B) 500 ft MSL C) 1,000 ft AGL Answer A. 400 ft AGL (structure exception aside). Q. A stable atmosphere is most likely associated with: A) cumulus clouds and turbulence B) stratus clouds and smooth air C) good visibility and gusts Answer B. Stable air gives stratiform clouds, smooth flight, and often poor visibility.
▸Exercise

Build your personal study schedule and a baseline.

  1. Take one full 60-question practice test cold and record your score per domain.
  2. Rank the domains by your weakest score; allocate study days proportionally.
  3. Make 20 flashcards covering every numeric Part 107 limit (altitude, speed, visibility, cloud clearance, registration weight).
  4. Set a go/no-go threshold (e.g., 85% on three consecutive mocks) before booking.

Quiz

Knowledge check
Q1. How many questions and what passing score on the UAG test? A: 60 questions; 70% to pass. Q2. Which two domains give the best study return on points? A: Airspace/chart reading and regulations - large, learnable, rule-based. Q3. What document defines the authoritative test content? A: The FAA Airman Certification Standards (ACS) for the Unmanned Aircraft General.

title: Staying Current, International Overview, and Insurance Basics
html:
The certificate is the start, not the finish

Passing the test makes you a remote pilot; staying legal and safe makes you a professional. This final lesson covers keeping your certificate current, a brief look at how the rest of the world (especially Europe) regulates drones, and the insurance every working pilot should understand.

Law.
Recurrent requirements, foreign regulations, and insurance mandates all change. Verify current FAA recurrent training, EASA rules, and any local insurance requirements before relying on this overview.

Recurrent training and currency

A Remote Pilot Certificate does not expire, but you must keep your aeronautical knowledge recurrent. The FAA replaced the old paper recurrent test with a free online recurrent training course that must be completed every 24 calendar months to exercise your privileges. Keep proof of completion with your certificate. The night-operations training is folded into the current recurrent material, so completing it keeps your night privileges current too.

Staying-current checklist
Complete FAA online recurrent training every 24 calendar months. Keep certificate, recurrent proof, and aircraft registration with you when flying. Re-check NOTAMs, TFRs, and airspace before EVERY flight - they change daily. Maintain Remote ID compliance and keep firmware/modules updated. Re-read Part 107 periodically; the rule itself evolves.

International overview: EASA and beyond

Outside the US, rules differ sharply, and a US certificate does not authorize you abroad. The European Union's EASA system is the most influential model. It is risk-based and organized into three categories:

  • Open category: lowest risk, no operational authorization needed; subdivided into subcategories A1 (over/near people, lightest drones), A2 (close to people with distance limits), and A3 (far from people). Pilots take online training and, for A2, an additional theory exam.
  • Specific category: medium risk requiring an operational authorization based on a risk assessment (the SORA methodology) or a standard scenario.
  • Certified category: highest risk (e.g., carrying people, large BVLOS cargo), regulated much like crewed aviation.

EASA also uses drone class identification labels (C0-C4) that map drones to subcategories. The lesson for a traveling pilot: always research the host country's authority - EASA in Europe, Transport Canada's RPAS rules, CASA in Australia, and so on. Never assume your home rules travel with you.

Insurance basics

The FAA does not require drone insurance for Part 107 operations, but clients, venues, and common sense often do. Two core coverages matter:

  • Liability insurance: pays for bodily injury or property damage you cause to others. This is the must-have; many commercial clients require proof of $1-2 million in coverage before you set foot on site.
  • Hull insurance: covers physical damage to your own aircraft and payload. Optional but sensible for expensive platforms.

You can buy annual policies or, increasingly, on-demand hourly coverage through app-based insurers - handy for occasional jobs. Read the exclusions: many policies void coverage for operations outside Part 107, flying without required authorizations, or beyond your stated parameters. Flying illegally can also void your coverage, another reason compliance pays.

Tip.
Before any paid job, ask the client what insurance limits and additional-insured endorsements they require, and get the certificate of insurance issued in their name. Sorting this out the night before a shoot is a recipe for losing the job.
▸Exercise

Build your professional currency-and-coverage file.

  1. Note the date your next FAA recurrent training is due (24 months from your last knowledge milestone) and set a calendar reminder.
  2. Pick a country you might travel to and identify its drone regulator and which category a typical photo flight would fall under.
  3. Get a quote (annual and on-demand) for $1M liability coverage and note the key exclusions.
  4. Draft a one-page pre-job compliance checklist: certificate, recurrent, registration, Remote ID, authorization, NOTAM/TFR check, insurance COI.

Quiz

Knowledge check
Q1. How often must a Part 107 pilot complete recurrent training? A: Every 24 calendar months, via the FAA's free online recurrent course. Q2. Under EASA, which category needs an operational authorization based on a risk assessment? A: The Specific category (e.g., via SORA or a standard scenario). Q3. Which insurance do commercial clients most commonly require proof of? A: Liability insurance (bodily injury/property damage), often $1-2 million.
